prompt:
You are analysing one document co-written by the AI-safety researcher Owain Evans, to find what DISTINGUISHES his research taste from the rest of the field. Output ONLY a JSON object, no prose, no code fences.

Document: "New, improved multiple-choice TruthfulQA | Truthful AI" (2025-01-15); kind=blog; his author position=first. For solo, first- or last-author work the choices are plausibly his; for middle-author work, mark attribution "team".

What we already know and do NOT want: he shares the field's consensus. Careful controls, matched baselines, hedged claims, replication, error bars, realistic setups, reporting rates, avoiding overclaiming, caring about safety. A blind judge already predicts all of that. Items of that kind are useless here, however well quoted.

What we want: his DEPARTURES. Places where this work makes a choice that a typical strong ML-safety researcher in 2025, facing the same problem with the same resources, would probably have made differently. The default you name must be a reasonable, defensible choice that competent researchers actually make (for example: study a capability with interpretability rather than behaviour; use the largest frontier model; build a broad benchmark; fine-tune only when prompting fails; frame the work around a threat model; avoid speculative or "weird" phenomena), never a strawman or a mistake.

Part A, "contrasts" (0-6 items; return fewer rather than include consensus items):
  dpoint: "Q" (which question or phenomenon to study at all), "D1" (experiment design), "D2" (which data, models, measurements), "D3" (accept or reject a result), "D4" (pursue or abandon a line), "D5" (how to read a surprising result), "D6" (what to claim, how to present it)
  default: one sentence, what a typical strong ML-safety researcher would do here instead
  choice: one sentence, what this work did
  why: the reason the document gives, or ""
  quote: a VERBATIM passage of 15-60 words, copied character-for-character from the document, that shows the choice. Do not paraphrase, stitch or fix typos.
  distinct: 1-3 (3 = most strong researchers would have taken the default)
  attribution: "own" or "team"

Part B, "axes": for each of these trade-off axes on which the document gives real evidence (skip the rest; most documents touch 0-4 of them), the pole the work leans to:
  - construct-scope: 1 = A narrow operational definition that isolates one sub-component of the behaviour. | 2 = A broad definition that covers the behaviour as it shows up in practice.
  - purpose: 1 = Informing a concrete decision someone has to make, such as whether a model is safe to deploy. | 2 = Understanding the phenomenon better, even if no decision depends on the result yet.
  - control-vs-realism: 1 = A controlled setup where one variable changes and the cause of any difference is clear. | 2 = A realistic setup with many natural cues at once, closer to what the model meets in deployment.
  - scale-vs-craft: 1 = Many variants, generated with a model and checked in bulk. | 2 = A few variants, each written and checked by hand.
  - elicitation: 1 = Maximum effort: the best prompt, scaffold and tools you can find. | 2 = Default behaviour: the model as users actually run it.
  - grading: 1 = An LLM judge over many transcripts. | 2 = Human or rule-based grading over fewer transcripts.
  - awareness-signal: 1 = Asking the model directly, after the episode, whether it thinks it was an evaluation. | 2 = Inferring it from the model's behaviour and reasoning during the episode, without asking.
  - items-vs-samples: 1 = More distinct items, one or two samples each. | 2 = Fewer items, many samples each, so you can tell an item that never trips the model from one that sometimes does.
  - evidence-bar: 1 = Re-test it on fresh samples before deciding. | 2 = Drop it and spend the budget on the next idea.
  - breadth-vs-depth: 1 = Move to a different direction. | 2 = Stay with it to find out why the results are mixed.
  - reading: 1 = Read a batch of transcripts closely. | 2 = Break the aggregate numbers down by condition and item.
  - explanation-prior: 1 = Look for a setup artefact before trusting it. | 2 = Run a direct follow-up that would confirm the effect, which also exposes most artefacts.
  - claim-scope: 1 = A narrow claim, limited to the exact setup you tested. | 2 = A general claim about the behaviour, stated with its uncertainty.
  - openness: 1 = Keep the items private, so future models can't train on them. | 2 = Publish the items, so others can reproduce and build on the results.
  item form: {"axis": "<name>", "pole": 1 or 2, "strength": 1-3, "quote": "<verbatim 15-60 words>"}

Part C, "new_axes" (0-3): other dimensions on which ML-safety researchers genuinely split and on which this work takes a clear side, such as how questions get chosen, empirical vs conceptual framing, preferred experimental paradigm, black-box vs white-box methods, model scale, toy vs realistic tasks, speed vs polish of release.
  item form: {"name": "<short>", "pole_a": "<one side>", "pole_b": "<other side>", "his_pole": "a" or "b", "quote": "<verbatim 15-60 words>"}

Return {"doc_summary": "<=2 sentences", "contrasts": [...], "axes": [...], "new_axes": [...]}

New, improved multiple-choice TruthfulQA | Truthful AI

# New, improved multiple-choice TruthfulQA

- January 15, 2025

Owain Evans, James Chua, Stephanie Lin

## TLDR

There is a potential issue with the multiple-choice versions of our TruthfulQA benchmark (a test of truthfulness in LLMs), which could lead to inflated model scores. This issue was analyzed by a helpful post by Alex Turner. We created a new multiple-choice version of TruthfulQA that fixes the issue. We compare models on the old and new versions and find very similar performance. This suggests that models are not exploiting the issue in the old versions to a significant extent, and so past results on the old versions are likely valid. Nevertheless, we strongly recommend using the new version going forward because future models may exploit the issue.

## Background

TruthfulQA, introduced in 2021, is a benchmark designed to assess the truthfulness of large language models in answering questions. The benchmark focuses on detecting imitative falsehoods: errors that arise from training models on internet text, such as common misconceptions or fictional concepts.

Each benchmark entry features a question with several correct and incorrect reference answers. Initially, TruthfulQA was intended for open-ended generation (not multiple-choice), evaluated through human labeling or automated evaluation. To support these evaluations, many reference answers were designed as paraphrases of other answers to ensure good coverage.

We also introduced a multiple-choice version of TruthfulQA called MC1, where one correct answer is paired with 4-5 incorrect options. In the original paper and codebase, this metric was computed by taking the logprobs for each answer and selecting the highest. However, it has become common for people to test models by showing them all answer choices at once and asking them to pick one. This setup can admit simple test-taking heuristics, such as selecting the “odd-one-out” answer (as discussed in Alex Turner’s post). In particular, if multiple incorrect options are paraphrases of each other, then a model can do much better than chance by simply avoiding these paraphrased options. This may cause the multiple-choice format to measure a model’s test-taking ability rather than its truthfulness. Our evaluations in 2021/2 suggested that models were not significantly exploiting such heuristics, but it remains a possibility with new models and different post-training and prompting strategies.

## New binary-choice setting

To address this, we’re introducing a binary-choice setting for TruthfulQA where the model is shown one correct answer and one incorrect answer, and asked to pick the correct answer. Here, incorrect answers were manually selected to target the imitative falsehood that we care about, while keeping them similar in format and length to the correct answer (where possible). This reduces the likelihood of the model relying on simple heuristics to select the best answer. The performance of various models on the binary dataset are shown below.

Performance on the new binary-choice setting for TruthfulQA for various contemporary closed and open models including Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, and Llama-3.2.

For the strongest model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet), performance is likely close to a human baseline. The original paper shows a human baseline for the generation version of TruthfulQA but not for this binary multiple-choice version. However, other models (including all the open models tested) show room for improvement.

## Comparison between binary and multiple-choice

Is it the case that models in the original multiple-choice setting were likely applying odd-one-out heuristics? As a simple test, we consider the relationship between the performance of models on the binary-choice versus the multiple-choice settings:

Plotting old TruthfulQA multiple-choice performance (MC1) vs. new binary-choice TruthfulQA performance for the same models as in the previous plot. The graph shows a very high correlation, with most models significantly improving on the binary-choice version and no model doing much worse.

If the additional answer choices in the multiple-choice setting provided useful information to help models narrow down the correct answer, we would expect capable models to perform better on the multiple-choice version. However, in practice, nearly all models perform better on the binary setting, suggesting that the extra options do not provide clear advantages.

Nevertheless, we recommend using the binary setting over the multiple-choice version to minimize the risk of models relying on “odd-one-out” heuristics and to ensure more interpretable results.

## Correlation between general capabilities and scores on TruthfulQA

When TruthfulQA was first released, large state-of-the-art models like GPT-3 showed inverse scaling, where they performed worse due to their improved ability to model the errors inherent in the pretraining data. However, as the plot above shows, highest-scoring models are now often the most generally capable ones (e.g. Claude 3.5 Sonnet).

This raises the question of how well TruthfulQA measures safety vs. capabilities in current models (see this paper). First, we emphasized that TruthfulQA covers only a narrow aspect of truthfulness, which is itself only one part of model safety. Second, the correlation between capabilities and safety is partly explained by model post-training (e.g. RLHF) that targets truthfulness. TruthfulQA depends on background knowledge (capabilities) and a truthful orientation (safety). If (hypothetically) all labs achieved strong truthful orientation via post-training, then a large part of the remaining variance across models would be explained by capabilities. But this would not mean that TruthfulQA is unhelpful: TruthfulQA (or questions inspired by it) may be a target during the development of post-training. (Note: It seems that models do not generally have a perfect “truthful orientation” from post-training.)

We also note that in recent models TruthfulQA performance seems to improve with scaling of base models (without post-training). That is, the inverse scaling trend does not continue even for base models. That said, we are unclear exactly what this correlation looks like for the zero-shot generation version of TruthfulQA when rigorously evaluated, and for the new binary-choice version (zero-shot). Nevertheless, base model performance is substantially below chat model performance at a given level of performance on standard capabilities benchmarks (MMLU, MATH, etc.), suggesting that post-training substantially improves the truthful orientation of models.
